introduction-stop-applying-from-laptops.core: Applying Terraform from laptops means unreviewed changes, long-lived admin credentials on personal machines, untracked versions, and state that doesn't match main. GitOps for IaC makes Git the single source of truth: changes arrive as pull requests, automation runs the plan and posts it, a reviewer approves, and only the automation, with scoped credentials, applies.

first_principles.problem: A Friday-evening laptop apply with an outdated branch reverts a colleague's fix in production.
truths: Git history is an audit log.

analogy.title: Bank transfers needing two signatures
analogy.story: No single clerk can move money from their desk; requests go through a logged approval system.
analogy.breaks: Banks have regulators; you must enforce branch protection yourself.

check.q: Why remove engineers' direct write credentials in GitOps?
check.a: So all changes must go through the reviewed, logged pipeline rather than bypassing it.

atlantis-terraform-in-pull-requests.core: Atlantis is a self-hosted server that listens to pull request webhooks. It runs terraform plan for affected projects, posts the output as a comment, locks those projects so other PRs can't conflict, and runs apply when an approved user comments `atlantis apply`. atlantis.yaml defines projects, workflows and requirements such as approved and mergeable.

first_principles.problem: Two PRs touching the same stack are both approved, and the second apply undoes the first.
truths: Plans must be visible in review.
Concurrent PRs on one stack conflict.
derivation: Apply **before merge** to keep main deployable.

analogy.title: A shared workshop sign-up sheet
analogy.story: Booking a machine locks it for your project; you show your plan to the supervisor before you start cutting.
analogy.breaks: Workshops have physical queues; Atlantis locks can go stale if PRs are abandoned.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Plan appears in PR; apply only after approval.

code.text:
version: 3
projects:
  - name: prod-network
    dir: envs/prod/network
    autoplan: { when_modified: ["*.tf", "../../../modules/**/*.tf"] }
    apply_requirements: [approved, mergeable]
    workflow: default

check.q: Why does Atlantis apply before merging rather than after?
check.a: So main only contains changes that actually applied successfully; failed applies are fixed in the same PR.

flux-tf-controller-the-kubernetes-native.core: The Flux Terraform controller (tofu-controller) runs Terraform inside Kubernetes. A `Terraform` custom resource points at a Git source path, and the controller periodically plans and, depending on approvePlan settings, applies automatically or waits for a manual approval of a specific plan ID. It brings continuous drift detection and GitOps-style reconciliation to Terraform code.

first_principles.problem: A team on Flux wants Terraform resources reconciled the same way as their Kubernetes apps.
truths: Flux reconciles from Git on intervals.
Terraform can run in a pod.
Approval can be tied to a plan ID.
derivation: Create a **Terraform** CR with path and interval.
Store state in a **backend** (k8s secret or S3).

analogy.title: A robot gardener with a schedule
analogy.story: It checks the garden plan every hour and tends what's off; for big changes it waits for your nod.
analogy.breaks: Gardeners don't need state files; Terraform still does.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Plans every 30 min; applies only when approved.

check.q: How does manual approval work in tofu-controller?
check.a: The controller generates a plan with an ID; setting approvePlan to that ID lets it apply exactly that plan.

branch-strategy-and-environment-promotio.core: Avoid branch-per-environment (dev, staging and prod branches): branches drift, merges get messy, and the diff between environments hides in Git history. Prefer trunk-based development with directory-per-environment on main and versioned modules. Promote by bumping a module version or copying a change to the next environment's directory in a new PR, so what differs between environments is visible in one tree.

first_principles.problem: The prod branch is 47 commits behind staging, and nobody knows which ones are safe to merge.
truths: Promotion should be a reviewable change.

analogy.title: One recipe book with per-restaurant pages
analogy.story: Each location's page lists which recipe version it serves; upgrading is a visible edit, not a separate book.
analogy.breaks: Restaurants might tolerate differences; environments should converge.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Prod change is one clear, reviewable diff.

check.q: Why is branch-per-environment problematic for IaC?
check.a: Branches drift and merges become complex, hiding what actually differs between environments.
